sourceAtom.label: Identify the sign of the derivative along a curve.

content.prompt: Identify the sign of the derivative along each curve.

spec.description: Downward-opening parabola; maximum right of the vertical axis and above the horizontal axis. No ticks or numerical labels.
spec.mathematics: Increasing before the maximum and decreasing after it.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied curve only; derivative signs are withheld.

answer.short: $f'>0$ left of the maximum; $f'=0$ at the maximum; $f'<0$ right of it.
answer.worked: Read from left to right. The curve rises to the maximum, where its tangent is horizontal, then falls. Hence the derivative signs are positive, zero, negative.

spec.description: Upward-opening parabola with minimum left of the vertical axis and below the horizontal axis.
spec.mathematics: Decreasing before its minimum and increasing after it.

answer.short: $f'<0$ left of the minimum; $f'=0$ at the minimum; $f'>0$ right of it.
answer.worked: The curve falls to the minimum, has a horizontal tangent there, then rises. Hence the derivative signs are negative, zero, positive.

spec.description: Cubic-shaped curve with a maximum left of the vertical axis and a minimum just below the positive horizontal axis; three horizontal-axis crossings.
spec.mathematics: Rise, fall, rise, with two horizontal tangents.

answer.short: From left to right: $+,0,-,0,+$, with zeros at the maximum and minimum.
answer.worked: The curve rises before the local maximum, falls between the two turning points and rises after the local minimum. Thus $f'>0$, then $f'<0$, then $f'>0$; $f'=0$ at both turning points.

spec.description: Cubic-shaped curve whose left maximum touches the horizontal axis and whose minimum is on the vertical axis below it.
spec.mathematics: Rise, fall, rise; the horizontal-axis contact at the maximum does not alter the gradient-sign rule.

answer.short: From left to right: $+,0,-,0,+$, with zeros at the maximum and minimum.
answer.worked: The curve rises to the maximum on the horizontal axis, falls to the minimum on the vertical axis, then rises. The derivative is positive, negative and positive on these respective regions, and zero at the two turning points.

spec.description: W-shaped curve, left minimum on the horizontal axis, maximum slightly left of the vertical axis and deeper right minimum below the horizontal axis.
spec.mathematics: Fall, rise, fall, rise with three stationary turning points.

answer.short: From left to right: $-,0,+,0,-,0,+$; zero at each turning point.
answer.worked: The curve falls to the first minimum, rises to the maximum, falls to the second minimum, then rises. The derivative therefore has signs negative, positive, negative, positive on those regions, and is zero at all three turning points.

spec.description: Curve descends to a minimum right of the vertical axis, then rises through a horizontal stationary inflection on the positive horizontal axis.
spec.mathematics: Negative derivative before the minimum, positive afterwards except for zero at the stationary inflection.

answer.short: $f'<0$ before the minimum; $f'=0$ there; $f'>0$ afterwards except $f'=0$ at the horizontal stationary inflection.
answer.worked: The curve falls to its minimum and then rises. Its tangent is horizontal at both the minimum and the flattened point on the horizontal axis. At the latter point the derivative is zero but remains positive on either side.

spec.description: Separate reciprocal-shaped branches in quadrants I and III, approaching both axes without touching.
spec.mathematics: Each branch decreases throughout; the function is undefined at the vertical asymptote.

answer.worked: Each branch falls as $x$ increases, so its tangent gradient is negative throughout. There is no point on the curve at $x=0$, so no derivative there.

spec.description: Increasing exponential-shaped curve above the horizontal axis, approaching it to the left.
spec.mathematics: Positive tangent gradient throughout; approaching a horizontal asymptote does not create a stationary point.

answer.worked: The curve rises throughout, so every tangent has positive gradient. It approaches the horizontal axis to the left without becoming stationary.

spec.description: Two increasing branches separated by the vertical axis; left branch crosses the negative horizontal axis, right branch crosses the positive horizontal axis.
spec.mathematics: Positive gradient on each branch, with no derivative at the separating vertical asymptote.

answer.worked: Both branches rise from left to right, so their tangent gradients are positive. The curve is undefined on the vertical asymptote $x=0$, so the derivative is undefined there.

spec.description: Oscillating curve through the origin while rising, with three visible minima and three visible maxima; both visible end segments descend.
spec.mathematics: Alternating signs according to rising and falling arcs; zero at six visible turning points.

answer.short: $f'>0$ on rising arcs, $f'<0$ on falling arcs and $f'=0$ at each of the six visible turning points.
answer.worked: Read left to right: the nonzero signs alternate $-,+,-,+,-,+,-$. At every change between rising and falling, the tangent is horizontal, so the derivative is zero.

spec.description: Single smooth hump above the horizontal axis, maximum on the vertical axis and flattening tails at equal positive height.
spec.mathematics: Positive derivative left of the maximum, zero at it, negative right of it.

answer.worked: The curve rises to its maximum on the vertical axis, has a horizontal tangent there, then falls. The flattening tails do not supply additional stationary points.

spec.description: Left branch rises through the negative horizontal axis towards the vertical asymptote. Right branch falls from above to a minimum above the horizontal axis, then rises.
spec.mathematics: Positive derivative on the left branch; negative, zero, positive across the right branch's minimum.

answer.short: Left branch: $f'>0$. Right branch: $f'<0$ before the minimum, $f'=0$ at it, $f'>0$ after it. Undefined at $x=0$.
answer.worked: The left branch rises throughout. The right branch falls to a horizontal minimum, then rises, giving negative, zero and positive derivative respectively. There is no derivative at the vertical asymptote $x=0$.

at a point; it can be either increasing, decreasing, or stationary.

inlines.text: Why do we need to find the derivative first?

answer.worked: The derivative gives the gradient of the tangent. Its sign determines the curve’s behaviour at the point.
The curve is increasing when $f'(x)>0$, so the tangent has positive gradient.
The curve is decreasing when $f'(x)<0$, so the tangent has negative gradient.
The curve is stationary when $f'(x)=0$, so the tangent is horizontal.

content.prompt: Find the stationary points of these functions. Check using Desmos.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=2x+8\end{align*}$$
Let $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{align*}2x+8&=0\\2x&=-8\\x&=-4\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}f(-4)&=(-4)^2+8(-4)+16\\f(-4)&=0\end{align*}$$
The stationary point is $(-4,0)$. In Desmos, the graph of $y=x^2+8x+16$ has a horizontal tangent at $(-4,0)$.

$$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=3x^2-48\end{align*}$$
Let $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{align*}3x^2-48&=0\\3x^2&=48\\x^2&=16\\x&=\pm4\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}f(-4)&=(-4)^3-48(-4)-7\\f(-4)&=121\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}f(4)&=4^3-48(4)-7\\f(4)&=-135\end{align*}$$
The stationary points are $(-4,121)$ and $(4,-135)$. In Desmos, the graph of $y=x^3-48x-7$ has horizontal tangents at both points.

$$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=4(x-2)^3\end{align*}$$
Let $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{align*}4(x-2)^3&=0\\(x-2)^3&=0\\x&=2\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}f(2)&=(2-2)^4\\f(2)&=0\end{align*}$$
The stationary point is $(2,0)$. In Desmos, the graph of $y=(x-2)^4$ has a horizontal tangent at $(2,0)$.

For $x\ne0$,
$$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=\frac{x^2-2x(x-1)}{x^4}\\f'(x)&=\frac{-x^2+2x}{x^4}\\f'(x)&=\frac{2-x}{x^3}.\end{align*}$$
Let $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2-x}{x^3}&=0\\2-x&=0\\x&=2\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}f(2)&=\frac{2-1}{2^2}\\f(2)&=\frac14\end{align*}$$
The stationary point is $\left(2,\frac14\right)$. In Desmos, the graph of $y=(x-1)/x^2$ has a horizontal tangent at this point.

content.prompt: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of each function.

answer.worked:
$$y'=2x-2$$
At a stationary point, $y'=0$.
$$\begin{align*}2x-2&=0\\2x&=2\\x&=1\\y(1)&=1^2-2(1)\\y(1)&=-1\end{align*}$$

$$y'=2x-4$$

$$\begin{align*}2x-4&=0\\2x&=4\\x&=2\\y(2)&=2^2-4(2)+3\\y(2)&=-1\end{align*}$$
The stationary point is $(2,-1)$.

$$y'=2x+6$$

$$\begin{align*}2x+6&=0\\2x&=-6\\x&=-3\\y(-3)&=(-3)^2+6(-3)+9\\y(-3)&=0\end{align*}$$
The stationary point is $(-3,0)$.

$$y'=4x-16$$
At a stationary point, $y'=0$.
$$\begin{align*}4x-16&=0\\4x&=16\\x&=4\\y(4)&=2(4)^2-16(4)\\y(4)&=-32\end{align*}$$
The stationary point is $(4,-32)$.

Breakdown: In particular, p10-q9-g includes the origin on the function but has no finite derivative there; p10-q9-i requires excluding both endpoints from the derivative's domain. Signs and stationary-point rules do not supply these decisions.
Checked: The earlier disconnected-branch questions concern derivative signs, and neither p5 demonstration nor p6 models a vertical tangent or an unbounded derivative.
Assumes: Students must sketch qualitative derivative behaviour near the displayed boundaries, without differentiating supplied formulas.
Also affects: p10-q9-f, p10-q9-g, p10-q9-h, p10-q9-i
Proposed repair (add-teaching): Before p10-q9-c add: “As positive tangent gradients grow without bound, f'(x) rises without bound; as negative tangent gradients grow in magnitude without bound, f'(x) falls without bound. A vertical tangent has no finite derivative.” At p10-q9-g demonstrate with three tangents approaching the origin from the right: “Their positive gradients grow without bound. The derivative is defined only for x>0 and rises without bound near 0.”
Done when: Students have a model connecting increasingly steep tangents to unbounded derivative values and excluding vertical-tangent endpoints.

[Pedagogy review · Suggestion · extension · pf-5ea755777e]
Idea: Extend the existing derivative sketch to vertical translation and reflection.
Why: The follow-up distinguishes function height from tangent gradient using the existing graph.
Proposed addition: Add (e) “Let g(x)=f(x)+3. Sketch g'(x).” Answer: the same sketch as in (d), with zeros at -1 and 1. (f) “Let h(x)=-f(x). Sketch h'(x).” Answer: reflect the sketch from (d) in the x-axis; negative outside [-1,1], positive between -1 and 1, and zero at both endpoints. (g) “Why does adding 3 leave the derivative unchanged?” Answer: vertical translation does not change tangent gradients.

[Pedagogy review · Suggestion · variation-sequence · pf-6cc7db0f36]
Idea: Add a short constant-term variation to expose unchanged increasing intervals.
Why: The run holds the quadratic and linear coefficients fixed while changing function height; the final item breaks that pattern.
Proposed addition: Add the single instruction “Predict before calculating.” Add (e) y=x²-4x-5; (f) y=x²-4x; (g) y=x²-4x+9; followed by (h) y=x²+4x+9. Answers for (e)–(g): y'=2x-4, increasing for x>2. Answer for (h): y'=2x+4, increasing for x>-2.
